video.title: I built this website in 8 hours with Claude. Now it makes $40K/month

summary: Starter Story host Gus interviews Frank Michael Smith, a non-technical sports creator who built Geogames (Geosports, Geohistory and others), a daily five-question map-tap trivia web game, in about eight hours with Claude. He claims about $40K/month (roughly $30-35K programmatic ads plus about 1,800 Pro subs via Stripe) and 700K monthly active users. Growth came from word-of-mouth sharing (53% share rate), playability inside X, and a 'host' programme where sports personalities write the daily questions and retweet. Key takeaways: build for web, build in shareability, start now, and stay in the game long-term.

speakers.name: Frank Michael Smith
speakers.description: Independent sports creator (about 4M followers) and founder of Geogames/Geosports

ideas.name: Geogames (Geosports and spin-offs): daily geography trivia web game
ideas.one_liner: A free daily five-question 'tap where it happened' map game, themed by niche (sports, history, etc.), monetised by programmatic ads and a Pro subscription.
ideas.business_model: Programmatic ad revenue plus Pro subscription (Stripe); free viral web game.
ideas.customer: Casual players and sports fans who share scores in group chats and on X; niche variants for history and other interests.
ideas.problem: People want a quick, habitual, shareable daily game; existing map-tap game had no sports or trivia twist.
ideas.offer: Free daily web game with five clue-based questions, tap on a globe, scored by closeness, shareable results; Pro subscription for extras (not detailed).

pricing.notes: Pro price not stated. About 1,800 Pro subs claimed.

acquisition_channels.details: Daily post of one question on X and Instagram story from founder's accounts; about 2,000 clicks/day (about 2% of traffic). Launch via a reply to his own NBA tweet went viral (40K players, then 150K in one day).

quote.text: I replied to my own tweet saying, hey, by the way, I made this game. I'd really appreciate if you guys all checked it out. And that reply went completely viral.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

acquisition_channels.details: Built-in score sharing; 53% of daily players share their score; about 98% of traffic is word of mouth via group chats.

quote.text: We have a 53% organic share rate, which means that we have, you know, 100,000 people who play around in a given day
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

acquisition_channels.details: 'Host' role: DM sports media personalities and athletes who engaged with the game; they write the five daily questions, and the founder posts announcing them, so they retweet to their audience.

quote.text: I created this new role called a hosting role, specifically designed for sports media personalities and athletes on the platform.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

acquisition_channels.details: Founder has about 4M followers, but claims only about 2% of traffic comes from his own posts.

ideas.delivery: Web app hosted on Vercel; questions stored in Google Sheets; leaderboards and stats in Upstash Redis; globe rendered with MapLibre; no app install needed. Questions are written daily by the founder or guest hosts.
unit_economics_claims: Tech stack costs low (Claude Max 20x, Vercel Pro)
ideas.startup_cost: Low: Claude Max 20x, Vercel Pro, domain; exact amounts not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated precisely; reached about $2K/month early and $40K/month within about three months of launch.

acquisition.how: Share mechanic is built in and traffic is organic; the host DMs and daily social posts are human-led and DMs to individuals need care under PECR. Agents could draft posts and manage host outreach.

onboarding.how: Players need no teaching and no signup to play; the game is self-explanatory.

delivery.how: The daily questions could be generated and QA'd by agents with a human check (or by guest hosts); hosting and scoring are fully automated software.

billing.how: Stripe subscriptions and programmatic ads are automated.

support.how: A consumer game with few support needs; an agent can handle the occasional subscription or bug query.

uk_applicability.notes: Web games, ads and Stripe work the same in the UK. Add cookie consent (PECR/UK GDPR) for programmatic ads. Sports-team trivia content should avoid trademark or logo misuse.

risks: Virality may decay and retention is unproven long-term
Ad revenue depends on programmatic networks and traffic
Easily cloned (it is itself a remix of Map Tap)
Revenue figures are self-reported and unverified
Sports trivia may raise IP concerns with team and league content

tactics.name: Build shareability into the product
steps: Make results a shareable score (e.g. colour-coded dot and score out of 100)
Keep the game playable with no signup or install
Make it playable inside the social platform where it spreads (X)
Keep the game so simple that nobody needs teaching

quote.text: make your product shareable. This sounds obvious, but it's not so geosports is only a success because of word amount.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

tactics.name: Guest 'host' programme with influencers
steps: Watch for large-following accounts who like or play the game
DM them offering a 'host' role
Host writes the five daily questions
When their questions go live, post announcing them as host
They retweet, exposing the game to their audience

quote.text: I DM people with large followings who have been liking the post about the game.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

tactics.name: Stealth launch then amplify
steps: Send to family and friends first and check whether they share it
If they share, post on social stories
Attach the pitch as a reply to an existing post
Prepare for retention once traffic spikes

quote.text: I sent it to a couple family members, friends, and I noticed that they were sharing it.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

tactics.name: Build a non-technical app with an LLM
steps: Have Claude research a reference product and write a spec
Block eight uninterrupted hours
Refer back to the spec whenever stuck
Screenshot confusing screens (e.g. Vercel) and ask the LLM to explain and verify
Ask the LLM to recommend tools to install

quote.text: I relied on screenshots and tons of questions and recommend everyone else do the same.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

tactics.name: Remix a successful existing product with a niche twist
steps: Find a game or app you love (Map Tap)
Identify what it lacks (no trivia, no sports)
Build your own version for your niche audience
Spin off the same engine to other niches

quote.text: I thought I could do my own thing and make a remix of sorts
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

tools_mentioned.purpose: Main distribution platform; game playable in-feed

warnings.warning: The launch was unprepared on retention; a viral spike on a five-day-old game forced rapid work on getting players to return.

quote.text: we were also very unprepared on the retention side
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

warnings.warning: The LLM was not always correct; verify outputs, especially setup steps like hosting and domains.

quote.text: the cloud didn't always get it right, but I got it right most of the time.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

warnings.warning: Objection that success is only due to a big audience: the founder says audience helps, but the game's growth is mostly word of mouth. The audience advantage should still be discounted when copying this.

lessons.lesson: Build sharing into the core loop (score cards, stats, one-tap share); word of mouth carried about 98% of traffic.

quote.text: 98% of the traffic is from word of mouth because the product is shareable.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

lessons.lesson: Zero-friction web products that work inside the platform where they spread (no app install, no signup) maximise virality.

quote.text: there is near zero friction. People could play this
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

lessons.lesson: Remixing a proven product with a niche twist is a fast route to an idea with built-in demand.
LLMs let non-technical founders ship a working product in a weekend; block out a full day and use the LLM for every blocker, including screenshots of confusing UIs.

quote.text: Try to block off eight hours uninterrupted work to give yourself a chance to build something.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

lessons.lesson: Daily habitual products compound: retention from daily play drives both ad inventory and subscription conversion.
Partner with people who already have audiences (hosts) by giving them a creative role and exposure, rather than paying for ads.

quote.text: This still feels like a cheat code that people are willing to do this
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

lessons.lesson: Ads can dominate revenue for high-traffic consumer games (about 75-85% here), with subscriptions as a smaller add-on.
Long-run persistence and skill stacking (13+ years in content before success) underpin 'overnight' wins; survivorship bias applies to such stories.

quote.text: I knew that you had to be patient. You have to keep your feet in the water.
quote.speaker: Frank Michael Smith

lessons.lesson: Founders with distribution skills have an edge now that building is cheap; building an audience, even a small one in public, is still advised.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand founder with a screen-shared dashboard (ads, Stripe) and consistent figures, but the numbers are self-reported and unverified. The transcript is Whisper-tiny with some mis-heard words, and the founder's large existing audience and the interview's hype framing limit how replicable it is. Revenue split and Pro price are not given precisely.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Starter Story promotes its own research platform and a free database of 100+ business ideas; the host has an incentive to showcase success stories.
